subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN WINNIPEG TRIBUNE
CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT-REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN WINNIPEG TRIBUNE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In an article in the Winnipeg Tribune dated May 1 of this year, questionable and unfair motives were imputed to me, and I wish now to deny them emphatically. I want to make it clear that the appreciation of my responsibility as a representative of the people, and that alone, is the motive that prompted me to expose the numerous adverse and detrimental effects that bill No. 5 would have on the Canadian wheat board and, ultimately, on the farmers of western Canada.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I gave you notice of my intention to speak on that bill at the last session, but that the time expired before my turn came. Any suggestion that I took the floor last Tuesday to talk out Bill No. 5 is totally unfounded, untrue and unfair. I still have six minutes to go when this debate is resumed, and I propose to avail myself
of those few minutes to make my position perfectly clear. I hope Mr. Dick Sanburn will then be in the gallery to listen.

maintopic: HOUSING-APPLICATION OF ACT TO FARMERS AND RESIDENTS OF TOWNS AND VILLAGES
speechtext:
Perhaps the house will permit me to answer a question asked the other day by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross):
I would like to ask the Minister of Reconstruction a question. Will he indicate to the house the arrangements which have been made to en-

Business oj the House-Precedence
able farmers and residents of towns and villages to take advantage of part 3 of the National Housing Act.
The answer is that lending institutions are authorized to operate under part 3 of the National Housing Act and will accept applications for loans from farmers. Part 3 of the act does not apply to loans to residents of towns and villages. Such loans fall under part 1 of the National Housing Act and the lending institutions are authorized to accept applications for these loans.
It is recognized that administrative difficulties and problems of inspection and appraisal have tended to make the lending institutions reluctant to enter outlying areas, and consequently coverage under the National Housing Act has not been all that could be desired. Recently the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has secured agreement from the major lending institutions for better coverage and it now appears that the fullest cooperation will be forthcoming from the lending institutions to ensure a complete coverage in these areas.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER MAY 8

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER MAY 8
speechtext:
That on and after Wednesday the 8th May to the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence on Wednesdays over all business except introductions of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
He said: I have put this motion on the order paper largely to allow hon. members to express their own views if they so desire, but primarily for the purpose of meeting what I believe is the general wish of the house to get on with its business as rapidly as possible. I recall that when I introduced the motion with respeet to taking Mondays the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) suggested that when we considered Wednesdays again the government should perhaps give a little more latitude than it otherwise would. No doubt that was my hon. friend's feeling at the time. But I am sure that hon. members will realize that we are getting on into the months of the session now and I would say that in regard to practically all the questions that come up on private members' motions there are other opportunities during the session where hon. members can discuss these particular questions, as for example, on the estimates, in connection with some of the public bills that come before the house, and the like.
The experience thus far this session has not shown that discussions on private members' resolutions on Wednesdays have led us very
far. I do not wish to press this motion at the moment, if there is any strong objection to it. I shall be prepared to modify its wording to accord with what appears to be the wish of the house; but I hope hon. members see the wisdom of getting on with government business if they really are concerned about not having the work of the session run too far into the months of this year.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER MAY 8
speechtext: Speaking for this party I may say we shall be glad to support the motion of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER MAY 8
speechtext:
We decided last week that we would support a similar motion, but I should like to add this word, that we did that before last Friday evening. Between eight and nine o'clock last Friday evening I think we all felt that the time of the house was not being occupied in the manner in which it should be. I make this mild protest in that regard, but we are anxious to facilitate the business of the house.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): The house surely has the support of this group in facilitating the business. Having in mind, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has, the way in which private members' hours have degenerated until they are practically useless, I suggest we support the motion.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTION AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER MAY 8
speechtext:
I am the first private member to rise to speak on this motion. The Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition are certainly not back-benchers; neither is the leader of the C.C.F., nor the leader of the Social Credit party.	.
It is not easy for a government supporter to oppose a government measure, and it is especially difficult when the measure is personally sponsored by the Prime Minister. 1 should like to be regarded, however, not as a private member differing from his leader, but rather as a private member differing at the moment from government policy.
The standing orders set aside Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays for the first four weeks of the session as private members' days. During the war we gave up that right because government business came first. In the first session after the war we gave up the right completely; and in this session, of the first four Thursdays the first three were devoted to the speech from the throne, which after all wTas government business. It is quite true that a private member had wide latitude in speaking on the address, but as government business had priority with the consent of the house, it left us only one Thursday for the

Business of the House-Precedence
discussion of private members' business. Shortly afterwards the Prime Minister put a motion on the order paper asking that Wednesday be given up. When the motion came before the house on April 9, the word "Wednesday" was changed to "Monday"; therefore we lost a full day instead of a half day, and once again the members of the house all agreed that government business should have priority. Now we are asked to give up our last effective afternoon, because one hour on Tuesdays and Fridays for private members' bills is not the same as two and a half hours on Wednesday. The argument used, of course, is first of all that government business should have priority. In that we have shown a fair measure of agreement, because we have given our Mondays to government business. The second argument used by the Prime Minister is that there are other opportunities to bring forward the matters we wish to discuss, namely, on going into supply, on the budget, and on the estimates.
Of course the house will note that I am concerned because my resolution will be the first one to be cut off. If I speak on that subject on the budget or on going into supply I shall make my comments on behalf of the three municipalities in my riding which are concerned in the matter referred to in the resolution. The next speaker may speak, and probably will, on some aspect remote from that, and there is no obligation on the minister, either in supply or on the budget, to answer anything I have said.
If I wait for the estimates I can wait until the Ottawa grant of 1100,000' in lieu of taxes comes up for discussion; but that will probably be on some steamy, sultry night late next August or early September, when the desire of the house is not to listen to debate but to push the estimates through in order to get home. On the other hand if we do have an afternoon to discuss what to my mind is important-even more important now that the dominion-provincial conference has been temporarily adjourned-the financial relations between the dominion and the municipalities, and certainly the municipalities are the hardest pressed of any of the governments in Canada at the moment, then not only can I state my case on behalf of the hard pressed municipalities of Vancouver North, but other parties can state their case and the government must make a reply. This is public business; it is not just a private member's business.
I wish to give one other illustration of the need of private members' day. Several hon. members have said to us: "Why do you British Columbia members not present a concerted story on the Japanese problem in-

stead of sniping away at the citizenship bill, the labour estimates, and the army estimates?" One of the reasons, of course, is that we lack this opportunity. The other night the hon. member' for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) and myself presented an amendment which was ruled out of order, and one of the ministers sitting near me at the time said:	"If you
want to deal with that you should have brought in a private bill." Judging from the way things are going, if we had brought in a private bill it would never have seen thfe light of day.
My resolution was put on the order paper on the third or fourth day of the session. If a resolution which is put on the order paper on the third or fourth day of the session is never discussed in the house,, obviously a private bill introduced this week would also fail to be discussed here. The opportunity for logical and coherent discussion of a public measure which is not on the government's program, but is brought forward by a private member, is more important to the government private member than to the opposition. As a matter of fact I envy my colleagues from British Columbia, the young member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and others, in the opportunity they have to speak on government measures. The government speaks particularly on government measures, and we who are in the background must either praise or damn. If we praise too much, we may be called sycophants; if we damn too much we are called rebels; if we do both we may be called inconsistent. Generally we keep silent,

speechtext:
Since the Prime Minister has indicated that the reason he has introduced this motion is to give members an opportunity to discuss the matter, may I just take one moment? I am willing to vote in favour of the motion, but I do not like the idea at any time of doing away with private members' day, because I believe if this parliament is to be effective it must function as a democratic parliament, with members sitting here representing their people and not their party.

Business of the House-Precedence
It is stated also that this motion is made so that we may get on with the business of the house. What are we doing if we are not getting on with the business of the house? Surely that is what we are doing all the time. We have these private members' days, but under our present parliamentary procedure what do they amount to? They amount to just nothing, except to allow the private member to let off steam and enable him to go back and tell his constituents, "See, that is what I said." May I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to hon. members of this house, that it does not amount to a row of pins what a member says here on private members' days, and that goes for all of us; it goes for myself too. Unless there is some revision of our parliamentary procedure by which a private member can present a matter and then have it voted upon, we shall not have a truly democratic parliament. What we require is to have a vote on private members, resolutions and action taken as the result of the vote.
My own impression is that to-day parliament is subservient to the government. In a real democratic parliament the government should be subservient to parliament. But in the ultimate results here, that is not so. I object to a party parliament; I want a real democratic parliament. I believe that the private members' days should be democratically conducted, that decisions should be made on the matters brought before the house and the government told, by those decisions, what the people want.

As pointed out by the hon. member for Macleod, if we conducted these private members' days efficiently we might accomplish something, but as it is they do not accomplish much, and I should be quite willing to forgo them until we have a more democratic procedure so that we can get on with the essential business of the country.

At the present time it is the only opportunity that the back-benchers have to hear both sides of any current issue discussed, and I am sure that up to the present the debates on private members' days have been of advantage to the members and informative to the public at large. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am now in a
position to answer the questions asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata when this matter was before the house. I apologize to him for not having had more success in my attempts to answer his questions when the matter was before the house. I did answer some of them, but I must confess my answers were incomplete. To answer his questions completely will of course take some little time.
His first question, I think, related to the credit of the Netherlands East Indies, and was whether that country had been supplied only with money, or with some ammunition and arms; and with whom the Canadian government dealt in making this credit. The answer is that the Netherlands East Indies was not supplied with ammunition and arms but with funds for the purchase of ordinary commercial commodities in Canada. The deal was negotiated with the representative of the government of the Netherlands East Indies, and the agreement was signed by duly authorized representatives of the Bank for the Netherlands East Indies.
The second question referred to my statement that by 1950 the British would have wiped out their deficit and would be getting back to equilibrium, and then asked what about Canadian equilibrium. I referred briefly to this question when the bill was discussed by the house before, and explained what I meant by "deficit" and "equilibrium":	The
deficit I was referring to was not a budgetary deficit in the sense of an excess of government expenditures over government revenues, but an entirely different thing, namely, deficit or

Loan to United Kingdom
disequilibrium in the United Kingdom's balance of payments on current account. Let me put it a simpler way. During the next few years the United Kingdom is not going to be able to get enough foreign exchange from her exports to other countries, her earnings from shipping, insurance and financial services rendered to other countries, the earnings on her outstanding foreign investments, tourist expenditures in the United Kingdom, etc., to enable her, without borrowing, to pay for the goods and services which she will require from other countries, the interest on her foreign indebtedness and other current account liabilities to other countries. In other words there will be a deficit in her current account balance of payments, which will have to be met primarily by borrowing from foreign countries. This deficit will be huge in the first year or two, but is expected to decline to small proportions in 1949 and be wiped out altogether in 1950. That is what I was trying to say at page 766 of Hansard.
Canada of course has no deficit in that sense. On the contrary Canada is in better than equilibrium to-day, and we expect that over the next two or three years Canada will have surpluses of substantial size in her current account balance of payments. That, indeed, is why we are making these loans or export credits-to enable other countries to buy from Canada goods and services which they would not otherwise be able to buy, at least in the same volume.
I may add that if we do not make it possible to sell our surplus production abroad in the next few years, if we are not able to build up and maintain on a high level that export trade on which so large a proportion of our people depend for a living, then we are likely to be unable to avoid continuing to show very substantial deficits in the other sense of that term-deficits in the budgetary sense.
Another question asked by the hon. member related to the deficit in the British balance of payments not covered by the proposed loans from United States and Canada, and my statement on page 766 of Hansard that this remaining amount would have to be found elsewhere. The question was: "Does 'elsewhere' mean all the other dominions and the other countries of the empire?" I meant "elsewhere" in this connection to cover all other countries-all countries other than the United States and Canada.
The fourth question referred to a quotation I gave from the report of the United States national advisory council to the effect that in the United States-United Kingdom financial
agreement of December 6, 1945, the British agreed to the removal of trade restrictions within one year from the effective date of that agreement. It then went on to ask: "Then, what about our British preference in trade?" The hon. member also asked the same question again on page 907 of Hansard in connection with certain other quotations from my own address. The removal of trade restrictions to which the national advisory committee's report referred, did not relate to tariffs but to quantitative import restrictions -that is to say, import quotas and foreign exchange restrictions. The United States-United Kingdom financial agreement does not deal with tariffs, which are what are involved when you speak of preferences.
Again the hon. member asked "What payments did the United Kingdom make to Canada since December, 1940?" Well, if I .understand it correctly, it is impossible to answer this question literally because many thousands of transactions would be involved. In other words the United Kingdom-I am speaking, of course, of the country or the people, not just of the government-makes a mass of payments to Canada every day- using for the purchase of Canadian goods or services or the payment of liabilities here the Canadian dollars she receives from her export of goods to Canada, the ocean freights earned by transporting Canadian goods, the interest and dividends paid on her investments in Canada, the earnings from insurance and financial services rendered to Canadians, and the expenditures of Canadians and the Canadian government and armed forces in Britain. Since December, 1940 there has been a myriad of such transactions, and it would be quite impossible to catalogue them. However, what I think my hon. friend had in mind was the statistical information which one finds in a balance of payments statement, including the receipts to United Kingdom of Canadian dollars from exports and other major sources. These Canadian dollars were all spent in Canada, and they had to be supplemented by a very large amount of additional dollars from mutual aid, and so on, to enable Britain to make all the payments she had to make in Canada.

It will be seen from the table that the United Kingdom's expenditures in Canada totalled $8,365 million, and that in addition to the transfer of gold and United States dollars to 'Canada amounting to $254 million during the period in question the United Kingdom used $3,775 million for payments in Canada, which dollars were obtained from exports to Canada, interest and dividend payments, freight and shipping services, travel expenditures in the United Kingdom and Canadian war activities overseas and other current items.
[Mr. Ilsley.l
The hon. member also asked, as reported on page 907 of Hansard, "What about Canada?" in connection with the statement I made that-'
British policies wall influence and largely determine the policies of many other countries, including particularly the countries now in the sterling area and probably the countries of western Europe.
I think my meaning was clear. I was talking particularly of the great influence which British policies inevitably have on the policies and the economic prosperity of other countries,

Loan to United Kingdom
because Britain is the world's greatest importer. I was thinking particularly, as I indicated, of the countries of the sterling area and of western Europe, and I was trying to show that unless Britain were assisted and encouraged to follow a liberal trade and currency policy she would be forced into restrictionist and discriminatory policies which would 'have an extremely bad effect on Canada, both directly and indirectly-the latter because of the effect which Britain's course of action would have on many other countries which constitute good markets for Canadian goods.
Dealing with the proposed cancellation of the British commonwealth air training plan indebtedness, the hon. member asked, how can we expect any repayment of a new $1,250 million loan if one of our reasons for suggesting cancellation was "the conclusion after much consideration that repayment of this $425 million was beyond the United Kingdom's capacity to pay within any reasonable period." The simple answer to that question is that we could not expect repayment of both the book debt and the new loan within a reasonable period, but w'e did feel that the United Kingdom would be able to repay the loan-over the long period and on the terms stipulated-and we were convinced that the new loan was necessary if our trade interests were to be protected. Attempting to make the United Kingdom pay off the $425 million debt on top of the $1,250 million loan, we were convinced, would have placed an altogether too heavy burden on Britain's balance of payments.
Another question asked what about "the gradual and orderly repatriation of Canadian securities owned in the United Kingdom". I am not sure thal; I get the point of this question. In my address-see page 770 of Hansard-I described this process of orderly repatriation of British-owned securities which has been going on and the undertaking given by the United Kingdom that the proceeds therefrom would be used to pay off the interest-free loan. Already repayments had amounted to over $161 million, and if they keep up at levels of the recent past it should not be long before the loan will be entirely paid off. From September 15, 1939, to December 31, 1945, total repatriation of Canadian securities from the United Kingdom aggregated $990 million.
Finally, the hon. member for Temiscouata asked about the detail of the settlement of war claims. This is a very complicated matter, but I shall do the best I can to answer the question, even though the agreement regarding the settlement of war claims is not part of
the agreement before the house. It will be recalled that when introducing the legislation which is before the house I pointed out that the agreement on the settlement of war claims is a separate and distinct agreement from the one to which the house is now giving consideration. The agreement does not need to be made under the authority of special legislation; it can be made under the authority of existing legislation. I pointed out that the settlement agreement is essentially a measure to settle promptly and with a finality a large number of outstanding claims between the two governments, an objective which might otherwise take years to achieve.
As the house will no doubt realize, when the armed forces and the procurement departments of two countries have cooperated as closely and fully in the prosecution of total war over a period of six years as have those of Canada and the United Kingdom, there accumulates between them a large number of financial claims of various kinds. Some of these claims are simple in nature and definite in amount. This is true of the largest number of the claims covered by this agreement, and in such cases all that is necessary in order to reach a proper basis of settlement is normal accounting procedure.
On the other hand, many of the claims arising out of the war are more difficult to determine. In some cases, for example, the prices that should be charged for equipment or supplies cannot be settled in advance, and should be based on costs which it may take a considerable time to determine with accuracy. In other cases it is completely impossible to keep records of actual transfers, because they took place during the course of military, air or naval operations and it was not considered wise to interfere with these operations and to tie up the necessary man-power to the extent that would be necessary to keep accurate books. In still other cases, equipment intended for one purpose may be laid aside and replaced by other equipment, and that which is laid aside may be lent or transferred to other armed forces for use by them without waiting for negotiations regarding the terms on which the transfer is made. I cite these merely as general examples of the types of difficulty which one inevitably runs into, and as I go over the list of claims hon. members will see specific cases in which these difficulties have to be faced and surmounted.
There is, therefore, an inevitable lag in settling the financial consequences of all the various operations and transfers that are necessary in conducting war. The working out of these settlements might well have taken years and been the occasion of endless
Loan to United Kingdom

disputes over the nature, magnitude and validity of dozens of claims between Canada and the United Kingdom.
The Canadian, government and the United Kingdom government, therefore, came to the conclusion that it was sensible to survey without delay the large number of claims of various types the two governments had against each other as a consequence of the war, and settle them by a payment of a round sum forthwith. The results of such survey convinced both of us that the payment by the United Kingdom to Canada of a sum of $150 million would be a fair and reasonable settlement of the balance of claims outstanding, and that on such payment all the claims as specified in the agreement could then be cancelled against one another.
The United Kingdom has now made this pa}'ment, the claims are cancelled, and we are proceeding to reflect these settlements in the various accounts in our books. The public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946, when they appear, will give a detailed record of these transactions and there will be ample opportunity for the house to discuss them in detail when the estimates of the departments concerned-army, navy, air, reconstruction and supply, agriculture, fisheries and trade and commerce-are being considered.
I might explain that the method we are following in order to make clear the process in our accounts is to establish what we call a United Kingdom general settlement account, to which are credited the payment made by the United Kingdom and the various amounts that would have been owing by Canada to the United Kingdom but for the settlement agreement. The account is then charged with the amount of the , claims which Canada has on the United Kingdom.
The simplest groups of claims covered by this settlement are those in the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Fisheries in respect of supplies furnished to the United Kingdom after September 1, 1945, when Mutual Aid ceased, and up to February 28, 1946, the end of the period covered by the settlement agreement. The amount debited to the settlement by the Department of Trade and Commerce, mainly in respect of wheat and flour, is $147,045,633. Similarly the figure charged by the Department of Fisheries for fishery products provided to the United Kingdom is $12,354,895. In both cases these amounts had been advanced under the authority of section 3 of the War Appropriation Act and the War Expenditures and Demobiliz-

ation Appropriation Act. Both amounts mentioned, as well as some of the amounts hereafter mentioned, may be subject to some slight revision before the books for last year are closed.
In the Department of Agriculture there were advances made on behalf of the United Kingdom for the procurement of agricultural products, mainly meat, eggs and cheese, of $113,604,894. In addition, there were cancellation charges on contracts for dehydrated vegetables which were cancelled on short notice late last fall, amounting to $350,000. On the other hand, the Department of Agriculture has a credit to make to the United Kingdom account of $2,600,000, on egg contracts.
The Department of National Defence for Air- has a claim against the United Kingdom of $12,736,060 in respect of the cost of training R.A.F. personnel subsequent to March 31, 1945. This was calculated on a capitation rate. On the other hand, there was a credit to the United Kingdom for equipment furnished in this training and in training Canadians in the same period, of $14,058,939. There are also credits to this account in respect of air force items of $14,225,873 for equipment purchased in the United States by the British air commission for Canadian account, and of $71,601,871 for the balance owing in respect of reserve stores and stores in pipeline behind R.A.F.. squadrons overseas. This last item must be offset by an amount representing the disposal value of these reserve and pipeline stores on hand at the end of hostilities on V-E day. While the amount of such stores is known or can be estimated, it has not yet been possible to determine a proper figure for the value of them, mainly because this value depends on the price at which such stores can be liquidated in the United Kingdom or elsewhere. There is also a charge to the settlement account, .now' reported at $24,034,421, for equipment originally obtained from the United Kingdom and for which payment was made in the first instance to the United Kingdom, but which in fact originated in other countries to whom payment will finally have to be made when the proper prices are determined. In addition, there is a considerable number of miscellaneous debits and credits on air force account, which result in a net debit to the settlement account of $27,653,358.
The naval accounts, although intricate in detail, present no great problems, and there are no large items still to be determined. The settlement account is to be debited with

Loan to United Kingdom
$12,351,048 for various accounts payable by the admiralty to Canada, mainly for services furnished by the dockyards at- Halifax. The account will be credited on the other hand with $6,938,884 by the navy for accounts payable by the navy to the admiralty, mainly for stores and services furnished overseas to Canadian ships.
In the case of the army, the major credits to the settlement account are a balance of $160,236,844 owing to the United Kingdom by the army for the maintenance of Canadian troops in the United Kingdom and in theatres of operations between April 1, 1943, and February 28, 1946. The payments in respect of all the supplies and services obtained by the army from the British army war office and other departments were made on the basis of capitation rates agreed between the two countries. It is impossible to keep records, particularly in the field, of all the equipment, ammunition, rations and other supplies obtained by the army, or to determine accurately rates of wastage and the proper division of costs for the various services provided by the United Kingdom to the army. There is also an amount payable by the army for initial equipment of $43,775,678, and an estimated payment in respect of westbound ocean passages for December, 1945, and January and February, 1946, of $6,000,009. On the other hand, there are debits to the settlement account of $27,037,768 for Canadian ordnance supplies transferred 'to the United Kingdom in the United Kingdom during the war, and of $91,997,769 for various types of stores supplied by Canada but covered under the general capitation rates for maintenance of the Canadian army, as already described. The. account is also to be charged with an estimated amount of $17,800,000 in respect of operating and rental charges for joint facilities in Canada. There are various miscellaneous debits and credits on army account, which add up to a total debit to the settlement account of $16,087,532.
I should draw attention to two large items which were offset one against the other and accordingly it was not necessary to compute a money value for the purpose of the settlement agreement, namely, Canada's obligation to the United Kingdom for reserve stores and stores in pipeline behind the Canadian army formations in Europe and Canada's claim on the United Kingdom in respect of certain ram tanks which, after being taken overseas by the Canadian army, were subsequently turned over to British forces to serve as armoured troop carriers after turrets and guns were removed. When the detailed role 63260-78

speechtext:
I will not ascribe the word "forced" to the hon. member. The question was as to whether Canada should not have required the United Kingdom to sell her securities in Canada in order to finance her purchases here instead of getting this credit from the Canadian government, or as a condition of getting the credit. This matter was most carefully and fully considered by the government after discussion with the United Kingdom representatives, and the government reached the conclusion that if Canada forced the United Kingdom to liquidate her remaining assets in Canada in order to finance her purchases here, other countries would be led to follow Canada's example, and that our action and theirs in this matter would so damage the future balance of payments position of Britain that they would be unable to follow the trade policies which we wish to see them follow and which it is in their interest to follow if these loans are available. Consequently the government considered that the proper course to adopt in regard to these securities was the same as that adopted in 1942, that is, to see that no liquidation of securities would be forced on the United Kingdom but that in so far as United Kingdom residents sold Canadian dollar securities outside the United Kingdom, and in so far as any Canadian securities held in the United Kingdom were redeemed, the proceeds would be used to pay off the 1942 loan made by Canada to the United Kingdom. In this way a gradual, orderly and limited reduction in Canadian investments of the United Kingdom is achieved, and also at the same time and to the same extent, this 1942 loan is repaid.
Britain's overseas investments represent the fruits of the savings of many generations of British people, and the means by which Britain has participated in the development of the resources of many countries. These investments added greatly to the productivity of Canada and of other countries and. indeed, the speedy and effective development of Canada was only possible as a result of the large amounts of savings which Britain invested here. Britain's overseas assets correspond
in certain respects to the natural resources of other countries. Britain does not have great resources of her own, and is able to support her own large population only because she has shared in the development of overseas resources of other countries by providing machinery' and equipment and skill for the development of these, and in return has obtained an equity or a security from which it derives income.
Before the war the net income of Britain from these overseas investments was approximately $1 billion a year, and this enabled Britain to pay for foodstuffs and raw materials for the British people, since Britain has been unable to export goods to a value as great as the value of her imports. As a result of the war, Britain has had to liquidate $5 billion of her investments, and to incur heavy debts. As a result, her income from her overseas investments after the war will be very greatly reduced. If we reduced it further by forcing her to sell her remaining Canadian securities, we should thereby thrust such a heavy continuing burden on the British exchange situation that she would not be able to follow the trade policies and exchange policies that we wish to see her follow. Perhaps that is not a sufficient answer for the hon. gentleman.
Then the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency asked a question a few minutes ago. This was just a simple question which asked if there was anything in the agreement which obliged the United Kingdom to spend the proceeds of this loan in Canada. That question was raised before by someone, I think the leader of the opposition, and my answer was that the understanding was that Great Britain will use the proceeds of this loan for the purpose of purchasing goods in Canada. The answer I gave was this, as reported on page 931 of Hansard'.
It is true that it is not provided in this loan that the $1,250 million must be spent in Canada. It was considered that in the case of Great Britain this restriction was neither necessary nor desirable.
It is not necessary because we know that Britain's purchases in Canada, requiring to be financed by some means other than its current receipts from Canada during the period in which they can use this credit, will exceed substantially the amount of credit. If they use the credit for other purchases, they will need to use other funds for purchasing here, funds derived, for example, from selling to Canada gold or foreign exchange that Canada requires.
It is not desirable because in the agreement, through the operation of article Y, we require the United Kingdom to provide Canadian dollars to countries in the sterling area and to other countries in return for sterling which these countries acquire from their trade with Britain, in order that these other countries may be able
Loan to United Kingdom

to ti-ade with Canada. If we are imposing this obligation on Britain to provide Canadian dollars to other countries which need them for buying in Canada, then we should make it possible for Britain to use the Canadian dollars we lend her for this purpose.
I direct the hon. member's attention to the remainder of that column which I do not think it will be necessary for me to read.

I think the loan of $700 million was justified, and I think the terms upon which that

loan was made *were justified. I think that as these securities are tied up to some extent with this loan we should try to see to it that if they pass out of the hands of the owners in Great Britain, they pass into the hands of owners in Canada. As I said before, I should like to have seen them put up more or less as a pledge or collateral against this loan.
I do not want to see these securities pass irom the control of Canada-we have a certain measure of control, as it were-to the control of a foreign country. I named the United States because that is the country in which they might possibly be sold; I did not name the United States because I thought that country was more objectionable than any other country. I think that was the point the hon. member for Acadia had in mind and it was not answered by the minister.

When we begin to count noses we are drawing the line pretty close; and after listening to the leader of the C.C.F.-Soeialist party it seems to me it is very bad policy indeed to make a loan and then attempt to tie the hands of the borrower. It is not very long ago that we looked to Britain as the champion of the greatest cause which civilization had ever been called upon to defend. We weTe willing at that time that she should bear the brunt of the battle with what help we could give from our resources, and we poured out our treasure and sacrificed many brave young lives to defend their cause. I think we are overlooking one of the most important features of this loan, namely, that we in Canada should desire to make this loan as much as that Britain should seek to secure it.

Loan to United Kingdom
The minister has already referred to Britain's wealth in her banks in the nature of deposits and has explained that this, after all, represents only domestic wealth and can be used only as a credit for trade within the confines of the United Kingdom; it cannot be used outside the British isles; if it could, Britain would soon seek to discharge some of her obligations, even within the sterling bloc. Britain during the war became indebted to the sterling bloc to the extent of '$14 billion, and this will have to be paid.
But the thing which impresses me most about the proposed loans, particularly the loan they are seeking from the United States, is the undertaking given by Britain that she will seek to make it possible, within a year, to exchange dollars for sterling and sterling will be changed into dollars. In other words, Britain, I believe, could carry on without this loan, even though she had to tighten her belt, but her trade would naturally be developed within the sterling bloc, to which she is already heavily indebted. Britain has already obtained a credit from Argentina by saying in effect to that country, "You can use this credit wherever sterling is acceptable", and if necessary in the post-war period Britain may, as I say, have to tighten her belt and do without things and make certain sacrifices but she will seek to repay her obligations. Not only will she seek within a year to make dollars exchangeable into sterling and sterling exchangeable into dollars; but if we grant this loan and if the proposed loan is granted by the United States of America she will be put in a position -where she can go to her sterling creditors and seek to pare down all her debts, which now are top-heavy and have a tendency to depress trade. I do not know whether all hon. members appreciate this, but I have lived long enough to know that the very life blood of a nation depends on trade. This is particularly true of Canada, which produces sufficient goods for from fifty to one hundred million people. If we do not secure some outlet for this production I do not know how we shall be able to keep trading with ourselves very long, because our granaries will soon be bulging again with wheat; our agriculture will languish, and our workshops will be closed. Unquestionably the post-war period offers a tremendous buyer's market. I w-as interested in noting that there is a great scarcity not only of what we refer to as consumer goods, but even of durable goods of the nature of rolling stock and machine tools. Many factories will have to be retooled for machine work in the post-war period.
Britain is the hub of the trade of the world. One-fifth of the world's trade in the prewar period moved in and out of British ports. We must seek to maintain that contact because, though Britain is in a rather rigid position to-day, she is very resourceful; and I may remind the hon. member for Temis-couata, in view of the reference made to the United States by some hon. members that when it was suggested that the United States should seek some concessions by way of military bases from Britain, the answer of the British was, either that the loan must be granted according to the terms already laid down, or, no loan at all. Those who can foresee the prospects of the future know that the world would face a grave situation were we to allow this to develop into a vicious trade war. and I see nothing else for it if this line of policy is to be pursued. My answer to the member for Rosetown-Biggar is, if you seek to have Britain pledge her securities that she may at present hold, I think it is a breach of good faith toward Britain; and I say to hon. members that we must be prepared to make this loan in a spirit of fairness, or otherwise we shall forfeit the substance for the shadow.

securities cannot be pledged ten times. They have been pledged for a loan of $700,000,000 which we have made, and there is an understanding between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government that they will not be sold to anyone but Canadians.

Wall Street Topics Canadian Pacific (From the New York Times)
The recent heavy trading in the common or ordinary shares of the Canadian Pacific Railway reflects in part heavy liquidation by British investors. These shares, held in the United King. dom. were not commandeered by the British government at the outbreak of this war. but holders were required to register them with the Bank of England. The hon. member for Calgary West is well versed upon these questions. I give him credit for that, but he must remember that General Smuts repatriated all the South African securities that there were in London. They are now owned by the Dominion of South Africa. He also knows that all the securities of the railways of India have been repatriated by India at the request of British people, not Hindus. Therefore they are the masters of their own destiny. That example comes from a great imperialist, General Jan Smuts and from the British people themselves who have made investments in India.
The question is, what is the difference if the securities are sold to the United States? I do not see any great difference if they are in the United States or in the United Kingdom. To me it is the same thing. I know I would be much more satisfied if they were held iu Canada by Canadians instead of being held by non-Canadians. That is a point of view which can be discussed. There is more interest in a company when it is entirely owned by the citizens of a country. There are numerous examples and I quote only a few to my hon. friend, who knows all about the matter. WTith regard to the Canadian Pacific railway, we have an interest in that and we must have a return of the stock here, of all these assets. They are ours. I do not see why some gentlemen in Great Britain, some lord or somebody else, should get all the profits from those securities.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
Is not one of the reasons "why the United Kingdom cannot dispose of those large deposits amounting to $44 billion *the fact that the savings certificates are attached to those deposits in Great Britain.
-Mr. ILSLEY: No. Let us suppose that an *exporter of lumber in Canada is prepared to take sterling for his lumber. He can get it all right. Sterling would be deposited to his credit in a bank in London, or somewhere else. What could he do with that sterling? Could he pay his men with it? Could he pay any of his bills with it? He has to pay everything in this country, in Canadian dollars. If he were to take sterling, then, so far as this country is concerned, that sterling would be nothing more or less than an I.O.U., unless our foreign exchange people converted it into Canadian dollars.
The existence of a great mass of pounds, shillings and pence in the United Kingdom owed by certain residents of the United Kingdom to certain other residents of the United Kingdom does not give the people of that country any value for the purpose of obtaining goods from other countries. What they must have is something different altogether. They must have liquid reserves, and we generally sum them up as gold or United States dollars. That gives them an external position. It gives 
them power to buy from abroad, to import and to live. That is the perilous position in which the United Kingdom is placed, namely the difficulty of keeping herself in a position where she has those liquid reserves. This great mass of internal indebtedness of one United Kingdom citizen to another United Kingdom citizen is not wealth, at all.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that it depends upon the ability of the country whose currency one holds to supply goods in return for that currency? Let me illustrate my point. The hon. member for Lethbridge, some other hon. members and myself were in Lisbon several years ago. We had very few United States dollars; but because we went via Newfoundland to Great Britain, most of us had a substantial amount of pounds. We found that when we wanted to get a small amount of Portuguese escudos, we could get a substantial quantity of the Portuguese money for a United States dollar. But when we tried to get something for the pounds we had in our pockets, we found all we could get was the equivalent of about two United States dollars to the pound. Why? Because the people of Portugal could buy United States goods with United States dollars. But they could not buy British goods with British pounds, because no goods were available owing to the war condition. In other words, the amount of sterling they held was so great that they did not want more of it. But they did not care about the amount of dollars they held, because they could get goods in return.
That is the same point we are now discussing. They do not ship sterling pounds; they ship goods. The money in the banks of Great Britain in the form of sterling is no good to that country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: So far as purchases abroad are concerned.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext: Where we go wrong, I think, is that we think in terms of money when we should be thinking in terms of goods. If we could only think in terms of goods we would have the key, but if we think in terms of money we become confused.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF FINANCIAL AGREEMENT SIGNED MARCH 6, 1946
speechtext:
It shows that history repeats itself, because we are going back to barter. Money has no value-a condition which I find extraordinary. But if it has no value, how is it that we have to supply some of our own?
I said at the start that the Canadian dollar was a blood donor to the sterling pound. It is just pump-priming now. There stands on the order paper in my name a question which, I suggest, shows the effect of that barter. We

Loan to United Kingdom
shall not be paid by pounds sterling; we shall be paid in British goods. The more we receive, the less we shall send.
This is what was said by the Minister of Finance a few days ago and I shall read it for the benefit of those who may not have read it:
Next year, that is in 1947, the amount of this deficit with Canada-
That is, the United Kingdom deficit.
[DOT]-will be reduced both because of lower expenditures of Britain here and because British exports to Canada will be at higher levels.
The minister seems to be reluctant to use the word "imports", when he says "lower expenditures of Britain here and because British exports to Canada will be at higher levels."
Because the minister stated at page 763 of Hansard the vital importance to Canada of the reestablishment, expansion and continued development of foreign trade, I asked this question:
Referring to the statement of the Minister of Finance, as reported at page 766 of Hansard of April 11, 1946,
1.	On what basis did he arrive at calculating "the lower expenditures of Britain here" in 1947?
That is next year. Naturally some orders have been given. Then my question continues :
2.	By "expenditures of Britain here" in 1947, did he mean Canadian exports to Britain?
3.	How did he figure out that they will be lower?

How did he calculate a higher level of British exports to Canada in 1947 as compared with what they were in 1946? Then, what will cause the 1947 level to be higher than that of 1946? Here is another: What goods are expected to be shipped from Britain to Canada in larger quantity in 1947 than in 1946? What goods are expected to be shipped from Canada to Britain in smaller quantity in 1947 than in 1946?
Those are the crucial points of the whole matter. During the war our shipments to Britain were unpaid for they were a gift. Shipments from Great Britain to Canada were paid for. That makes a great difference. Trade cannot be unilateral; we cannot go on making gifts like that indefinitely.
We are told that if these loans are passed by this parliament and by congress England will have money to buy. But it will be our own money that will be used. It will be a business proposition only when they start to refund the loan. Otherwise it will not be a business proposition; it will be a gift. If you
give a boy S10 and he buys something in your store, it will not be a purchase. You will lose money; you will not make a profit on such a transaction.
There is one point in the argument of my hon. friend to which I object most strongly. He says that England was our best customer during last year. We do not have separate statistics for exports that were made as gifts and for exports that were paid for. I asked the minister if it was possible to get them separately and he told me it was not. Therefore the Canadian public's idea of what our trade consists of is a mere illusion.
England is entering a period of reconstruction and reconversion, as are all other countries. It is said that if we continue as we have been doing our imports from Britain will increase and our exports to Britain will decrease. I cannot understand it.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a motion to go into supply gives an opportunity to members of the house to raise matters which they regard as of importance either to the house or to the country. I wish, therefore, to raise a question of major importance to the chief primary industry of this country and to the country itself, namely the inequitable position in which agriculture now finds itself and the lessened production as a result of that inequity. For the purpose of bringing this matter to the attention of the house I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), this amendent to the motion:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the motion be omitted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies."
I said the question I wished to raise was that of the inequitable position in which agriculture now finds itself and the fact that, for this and other reasons, production of farm products is going down. These are the reasons I am bringing this matter to the attention of the house.
Production in agriculture is lower now than it was last year, in dairy products, in poultry and in hogs, and it is still falling in all these three sections of our agricultural economy. In the beef cattle branch of the industry, while the supply is high, there is a bottle-neck in marketing owing to the price ceilings on beef, and their administration. There are price ceilings on beef but no price ceilings on live cattle or on the different grades of live cattle.
On the United States side of the 49th parallel the price of wheat, if we take into account the recent bonus of thirty cents and the increased value of United States exchange, is now equal to a dollar a bushel more than it is on this side of the line, in Canada. The result is that if that difference in price continues, with a normal crop of wheat in Canada the farmers of this country will contribute to the maintenance of this price structure a sum approaching

Price Ceilings-Farm Products
$200 million a year. I have referred to wheat because it is the largest of our agricultural export commodities. On Saturday last, two days ago, the price of No. 3 northern wheat in the United States just across the boundary from southern Manitoba was SI.68%; the subsidy of thirty cents brings it to $1.98%; then, with the exchange added of twenty cents a bushel, the value of No. 3 northern wheat at that point in the United States amounts to $2.18% a bushel. At the same time, at Gretna, Manitoba, just on this side of the line, the price of No. 1 northern wheat is $1.08 a bushel, to which of course would be added whatever may be the value of the participation certificate; nobody knows what that will be-possibly fifteen cents. I have compared the price of United States No. 3 northern with Canadian No. 1 northern because those grades are of approximately equal value. If we take the grades having the same name on the two sides of the United States boundary the difference is a little less. These figures go to show that at this moment the price of wheat on this side of the boundary line is nearly a dollar a bushel less than it is on the other side. That means that farmers are paying a disproportionate share of the cost of Canada's price stabilization policy. If we have 200,000,000 bushels or more to sell, and if that difference is maintained, it means a contribution of nearly $200 million by that section of our agricultural economy. My view is that there can be no justification for Canada holding down the price of its chief export commodity, wheat, to a figure almost a dollar a bushel less than the price received by our chief competitors on the other side.
With respect to beef cattle the situation is confusing. It is confused by the absurd method of having a ceiling price on beef but no ceiling price on the different grades of live animals. Since there is no grading of live animals we are finding now with the increased demand that the spreads between the different grades are not sufficient to encourage the production of high quality beef. We find that, while farmers who produce grass-fed cattle are not too much discouraged about the outcome, those-or many of them-who produce grain-fed cattle, who fed them last fall and through the winter are finding it impossible to sell them at a profit.
The commission men in the part of the world where I am acquainted report, as I have said, that producers of grass-fed cattle are not disturbed, but producers of grain-fed cattle cannot carry on except at a loss, and this view is commonly held-I express no personal opinion about it, for I do not know- that the few grain-fed cattle which are reaching that market now are to a considerable extent being shipped east to be absorbed into a black market. As I said, I express no personal opinion on that subject, but that view is commonly held. This policy on the part of the government tends to discourage the production of high quality beef. Those producing beef cattle find that the spread in price between the lower grades and the higher grades is now too small to justify the production of the higher qualities, and there is a growing feeling that if the government is to continue price ceilings there should be a dominion-wide grading system carried right back to the producers so that there will be price ceiling differentials on the different grades of live cattle.
With regard to other products, poultry production is also going down. It is expected that there will be a shortage next winter, not a shortage for Canada but a shortage in the total production The same is true of bacon. The suggestion is that we are not likely to be able to meet the maximum commitments made to Britain.
On the whole, farm production in Canada has been declining since 1944; 1945 was lower than 1944, and 1946 will be lower than 1945. I suggest that, if the farmers were given the necessary stimulus to produce, the situation would be greatly improved. The government should have been watching this situation more closely. It should have raised farm price ceilings in line with increasing costs of labour and other items of production. Not only are farmers' costs increasing, but in the case of farm labour they are finding it difficult to get it at any price. If these things had been done we wrould not to-day be faced with declining agricultural production.
Those are the two points I wished to lay before the house. The first is the inequity to farmers, with rising costs on one hand, which have not been adequately met by any price adjustments on farm products the government has made. For example, in the case of butter the price - increase was too little and came too late On the one hand, I say, we have rising farm costs and, on the other, farm prices not being adequately raised. That produces a condition of inequity. With shortage of farm labour and higher wages in other industries, farm labour is not returning to the farms in the way it might have been expected to do, in the way it did in days gone by; and when it does go back farm wages are twice as high and sometimes more than twice as high as they were.
These conditions combined are resulting in lessened production. In these days what we should be striving for is maximum production,
Price Ceilings-Farm Products

particularly in the field of food products. It is for these two reasons-inequity and decreasing production-that I have brought the matter before the house for discussion to-night.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The question which has just been raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) ought, I think, to be replied to at once particularly in relation to agricultural production. The broad statement has been made that agricultural production has been going down because of the prices policy of the government. I am not going to argue the question in regard to the effect of the prices policy on production in Canada, because the leader of the opposition himself has not introduced any proof whatsoever of the statement he has made. But some general statements have been made in relation to wheat and in relation to live stock products which I think should be answered.
The first is to the effect that the price of wheat is higher on the United States side of the line than it is on the Canadian. There is nothing new about that. One can say that the price has been higher on the United States side than it has been on the Canadian side at least ever since the war started. I am not sure how far one could go back and still have that statement true, but the price of wheat has been higher on the United States side of the boundary line than on the Canadian for a considerable time. Nevertheless we had a higher production of wheat in 1942 than we have ever had in this country with the possible exception of one previous year, and certainly the highest production per acre that we have ever had.
The most important phase of the question, however, is that the reason for the present price level in Canada is to try to conform with a matter of a policy which has been advocated by farm organizations, in western Canada at least, ever since I have been in the west, namely, since 1901, and, I believe, for many years before that. As a matter of fact, it was the chief thing that farmers had in mind when the Canada Grain Act was first placed on the statute books of the country, the thought being that some day we should desire to have a stabilized price for the most important commodity which is exported from Canada, and particularly from the west.
The first time we have ever had an opportunity to test out the possibility of having a stabilized price for wheat for the Canadian farmer is the present. To-day we are faced with a situation where Britain, who is the chief consumer of our exported wheat; France, who is perhaps the second greatest consumer 
of our exported wheat in normal times, and when they are not preparing for wars in Europe; Belgium, who is another large consumer of Canadian wheat; and Holland, are all approaching this government-and we are discussing the matter with them-to set up agreements which will give stability to the sale price to the wheat farmer of western Canada. In order to give an opportunity to have these discussions, we said during the last session of parliament that the ceiling price of wheat to those countries in the meantime will be pegged at $1.55 a bushel No. 1 northern Fort William. We have adhered to that position up to the present time, and during the intervening period these discussions have been going on.
If we are ever to obtain the results we started out to obtain on behalf of agriculture we must stay with our objective sufficiently long at least to prove whether we can carry through to the objective or not. It is, I believe, admitted by all farm organizations that up to the present time neither this government nor the governments of Britain, France, Belgium and Holland, with whom we have been negotiating, have had sufficient time to arrive at a final conclusion in connection with a proposal as far-reaching as this. In the meantime, however, we have been holding the price ceiling at $1.55.
The other side of the question is that while there has been some going up and going down of prices, one commodity that the leader of the opposition speaks of, and has spoken of most often during this session, is hogs. He says that hog production is going down. I suppose he is not aware that in recent weeks, as a matter of fact at the present time, the price of hogs in Canada, all things considered, is higher than can be obtained in the United States, and still the numbers of our hogs, as has been stated, has been going down. In other words, in one case, in the case of wheat, we are told that because the price is higher in the United States than in Canada and the price of wheat is going up in the United States as compared with Canada, that is the reason for our production going down or being down in Canada. On the other hand, in spite of the fact that hogs have been going up in price in Canada and going down in numbers, the price is down on hogs in the United States as compared with Canada.
The fact of the matter is that the weather and other conditions associated with the production of farm crops were quite different in 1945 from conditions in 1942 and 1943 and to a lesser degree in 1944. As I have said in this house before, as a result of that the production of feed grain, or at least the quantities

Price Ceilings-Farm Products
of feed grain stored in this country that are available to farmers with which to feed, have been going down, and farmers themselves have reduced the numbers of live stock to be fed to conform with these facts.
I come now to another question which was raised, namely, that having to do with dairy products. It was suggested that the production of dairy products is going down. As a matter of fact, we are milking more cows in Canada to-day than before. The cow is the source of the supply of dairy products. If we are milking more cows in Canada it is hardly right to state that the production of dairy products is going down as a result of any policy followed in this country at the present time.
The Minister of Agriculture of Ontario misrepresented the position the other night, probably unintentionally. He is reported to have said something in relation to the price of milk, that it had some bearing on the number of cows being exported to the United States, and that these numbers were greater than ever before. I recall that when that question was raised on the floor of this house some two or three years ago I rose in my place and said that so far as I was concerned, irrespective of what other members did, I was not going to advocate the setting up of any policy that would stop the export of cows to the United States. One of the best paying products that the farmers of this country have to sell to the United States is dairy cows. One of the export products upon which there has been no obstruction placed on the boundary line of the United States is dairy cows or breeding stock generally. Farmers who prior to the war knocked their calves on the head the day they were bom now feed these calves until they are two years old, breed them and sell them in the United States at profits in order to bring more returns to the farms in different parts of the country.
The records show that to-day we have more dairy cows than ever before in spite of the fact that we are selling more dairy cows to the United States than we sold before, or at least many more than we have sold in recent times. They are being sold at good profits which bring good returns to the farmers. In other words, it requires a great deal more than just a resolution or an amendment of the motion to go into supply to prove that the farming situation it is claimed exists to-day or any reduction in production is due to the price ceiling policies which have been followed by the government in relation to farm products.
The suggestion has been made that we have no ceiling prices on cattle. The leader of
the opposition knows, as I know, that there are very few farm organizations anywhere between British Columbia and the Atlantic ocean which have passed resolutions or given support to rail grading of beef or the grading of beef in the manner which was suggested a few moments ago. As a matter of fact, as I recall it, the province from which the leader of the opposition comes-and I think he associated himself with the objections-has been the chief objector to the rail grading of hogs, wThich has been pretty well accepted in other provinces right across Canada, and is still objected to by Manitoba. Some farmers in that area have objected to the rail grading of hogs, taking the position that it gives the advantage to the packing houses to have the dead hogs hung up in the packing plant before they are actually graded and before the price is set for them. These same farmers in season and out have consistently objected to the grading of cattle upon the rail. I doubt very much whether there is any other way in which cattle can be successfully graded than on the rail.
Let me repeat that farmers right across the country, from British Columbia to the Atlantic have been objecting. It is true that in the Fraser river valley we have been grading cattle on the rail for some considerable time. But that is a restricted area into which beef comes from outside for marketing as well as beef which is produced in it. All of it has to be graded. We have tried out rail grading there as an experiment with the idea that probably some day we may find it possible to have rail grading applied across the country. But when it is said that in setting the price ceiling for live stock the prices board is to be condemned because it did not place a ceiling based upon grading upon cattle, I, for one, am quite prepared to take some responsibility for the board not having done so, and I think every farm organization that knows the situation which existed in this country in 1941 will support me in that contention. The price at which beef sold at retail in 1941 was just as high as the price back in 1928 when the price of cattle was two or three cents higher than the price of cattle in 1941. Those of us who were following the markets in connection with cattle and beef at that time took the position that it would be absolutely unfair to the farm population of this country to have a ceiling put upon cattle as they were being sold in 1941 when ceilings were put on other commodities in this country.
Back in 1928 steak was selling at 48 cents a pound, and cattle were selling at twelve cents a pound. In 1941 the price of steak was 48
