Well, if they were not encouraged to produce I suppose the assumption would be that production was down, and it was down because of the fact that they had not been encouraged to produce, the result being that beef is not coming on the market at the present time. Beef did come to the market very freely until about three weeks ago, I think, and then this suggestion went out that farmers would be paid $10 a head less for their cattle when they came on the market. After that order was issued the farmers stopped delivering finished cattle to the market; blit this morning I heard it announced over the radio that for the first time in three weeks the usual numbers of cattle were coming back on the market. I presume they are coming back because at the end of last week prices were up again to around 13 cents, or 13J in some cases for the best finished beef, so that cattle are starting to move to the market again.
The point I wish to make is that these difficulties come up not because of the general price policy of the government in relation to farm products but owing to the fact that some persons take actions thej7 are not justified in taking, and possibly something should have been done about the matter. In any event the markets are righting themselves at pretty much the levels of three weeks ago. Production records for this year, however, cannot be judged by what has taken place in the first three months of 1946. As I stated at the beginning of this session, our grain supplies were down when we came into this w-inter season, and as a result feeding has been down during the winter. But no one knows what the position will be in relation to the feeding of livestock during this summer. It depends entirely upon moisture conditions right across the country and the amount of grass available, as to whether w7e shall have finished cattle coming off the grass throughout the summer, or whether we shall have more milk coming from our cows during the summer and therefore a greater production of dairy products of one kind or another. If we have good grass, with a greater number of cows than we have ever had before, cer-

Price Ceilings-Farm Products
tainly we shall have a greater production of dairy products than we have ever had before. On the other hand, if we have the usual acreage of wheat-and I assume we have that usual acreage or perhaps more than during the past few years-and if we have good rhins during the summer months, we shall have wheat and feed supplies again for the succeeding winter. But if these things fail to happen, in relation to both the amount of grass available and the feed supply, no change in price policy will produce more farm products, in the form of live stock and live stock products, than we have at the present time. This year we fed all the grain that was available in this country. We could not have fed any more no matter what had been the price for live stock products. Therefore I say to the house it was not the price policy that created any existing condition in relation to production.
As to butter, the other product mentioned, on a number of occasions I have said in the house that our production of creamery butter, which is the only butter as to which we have any real records, for the last three years has averaged more than 40,000,000 pounds more than during any previous three-year period in at least recent times. It is not the fact that production is down that makes it difficult to secure butter in certain places; it is the fact that consumption is materially up, and with consumption so much higher we require a certain control over the distribution of butter throughout Canada.
I make this reply, Mr. Speaker, in order to avoid having the suggestion go out that our agricultural production will be so far down this year that we shall not be able to supply the markets which are depending upon us for food this summer and next winter. This country is not going to gain by having any such impression go abroad at the present time. There are people who are absolutely depending upon us. They are reljdng upon this country to produce their food supplies for next year; but as soon as we convince them that we are not going to have the food supplies available there will be only one thing left for them to do, that is, search around the world to make certain that food supplies will be available to the greatest extent possible. Therefore I suggest that we are not doing this country a service by suggesting, in any speech made here or any resolution moved, that our production is in danger of going down to levels of which we have never dreamed, and that our farmers are entirely dissatisfied with their returns. I know they are dissatisfied to a degree with the returns in certain cases: but in all my experience with
agriculture in this country, extending back to 1901, I do not think I have ever known a time when more farmers have expressed themselves as being fairly well satisfied with existing conditions. That would not justify me in saying we should not do anything to try to improve their condition We should be doing that at all times. But to give the impression that we have no prospect of having food in this country with which to supply the markets depending upon us is not going to assist either the farmers of this country or those who in other countries are looking to Canada for food in the months that lie ahead. We shall get better results by supporting the policy which is being followed at the moment of dealing with governments elsewhere for the sale of our farm products at prices which will stabilize the returns to the farmers, and then asking the farmers to produce uader the price levels made possible by the arrangements entered into, than by anything else we can do. But if every time we get a stabilized price for any commodity we are going to spend the greater part of our time shooting at that price and saying that for the time being the price realized by someone else is higher, that is the surest way I know of to get rid of what the farmer has been asking for many years.
Those who are telling us to-day to empty our bins to the last bushel in order to do something or another; those who are calling upon the farmers to deliver as they have never delivered before everything they produce on the farms, can create a situation the very opposite to that for which we have been striving by our policies and for which the farmer himself has been striving. For example, suppose we entered into an agreement to deliver an average of 250,000,000 bushels of wheat annually to a group of countries for a period of five years. Suppose, before starting to do so, we had taken every bushel of wheat out of our bins, so that none would be carried over into the succeeding year. Then suppose we had a crop failure. There would be no possibility in the world of carrying out the agreement we had entered into. Experience over the last twenty years has shown that if we . carry on as we should in this country and produce 560,000.000 bushels of wheat when we can, under good weather conditions, and produce only 200.000,000 bushels in another year, when weather conditions are poor, our average production will be about 390,000,000 bushels a year. Experience has shown, also, that we can take our own requirements for seed, feed and food out of those 300,000,000 bushels and market about 250,000,000 bushels outside this country every year. But we cannot do that
Price Ceilings-Farm Products

unless we establish something like the ever-normal granary in this country. When we allow anyone, for any purpose whatsoever, to put over propaganda in Canada which takes wheat out of the bins of the farmers, in this or in any other year, and leaves the position such that if we had a crop failure we could not supply the demands of the countries dependent upon us in the years ahead, we would have destroyed forever the possibility of having stabilized farm prices for farm products in this country, and we have established again a situation where the only thing we can rely upon in connection with the sale of farm products is the process of speculation.
It is far more important at the present time that we should be able to establish a stabilized price of, let us say, $1.55 a bushel for five years, than that we should simply look over the United States boundary line and say that, because they were dealing with a special situation in their country under which they pay thirty cents a bushel additional, we should step into the same line of policy in this country, despite the fact that we have not followed the same policy which they followed in connection with price controls throughout the entire period of the war.
If we can have our stabilized price established, and if we can produce the quantity required during the next-year or two to supply the market we may agree to supply, then we have gone a long way toward establishing for the farmers of western Canada, in relation to wheat prices and wheat production, stabilized returns over a, long period of years. To me, thht is far more important than a price of $1.75 or $1.85 for the time being with the possibility of seventy-five cents in a year or two years hence.
We want prices stabilized, if we can do that at all; and we want the situation dealt with so as to assure that that can be done. It is most important that it should be done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not just follow the procedure of the house. When we moved into supply on the last occasion I tried to raise a grievance. The order paper carried my motion until last Monday, at which time it disappeared from the order paper.
However, I am not complaining about that this evening. I wish to have a few words to say on the motion introduced by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). I notice that the motion reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government's price ceiling policies with respect to farm products are discouraging production of needed food and imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.

I wish to make it perfectly clear that we have stood wholeheartedly and solidly for the stabilization of prices. I believe with those who accept the same point of view, that the farmer does not want a high, speculative price at one period and a low, depressed price at another period. He wants a price that is not a speculative price, but rather one which is based upon the cost of production, and which bears at least some relationship to the things he has to buy.
I agree with the amendment to this extent, that the farmers in Canada are being discouraged, and that we are imposing an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price policy on their backs.
But I am approaching the matter from an entirely different point of view. I am approaching it from this point of view, that if we are to have stabilization, then let us have stabilization. If we are going to say to the farmer, "The price of wheat in January is to be $1.55, and in May it is to be $1.55", then I say that if in January the manufacturer of agricultural implements states that the price of his binder is to be $281 or $320, or whatever it may be, it should be the same in May. We cannot expect one group in our society to accept a stabilized price for a period, and then have that ceiling broken for some other organization upon which the producer relies for his machinery.
So that I say the policy of the government in this respect is discouraging to the farmer, and it has placed an unfair burden upon the backs of the producers. The other day we had a discussion in this chamber about an increase in the price of agricultural implements. That was an increase to the extent of 12-J per cent, and without warning. That followed in the prairie provinces-and this affected my constituents particularly-an increase of two cents a gallon in the price of gasoline. This has been a serious blow, or, if I may use the plural:	These have been very serious blows
to the maintenance of our price ceilings; and I regret them exceedingly.
The leader of the opposition has discussed the matter of live stock prices. Well, it has seemed to me that the attempt to keep the ceiling on beef, and to accept no differential between, we will say, fall and spring prices, is unfair again to the agricultural producer. Grass-fed stock which goes on the market in the fall, is fed without either expensive grains or without the same amount of labour. Then, when the grain-fed stock goes on the market in the spring, after the long winter and the hard work involved in looking after that stock, we find the farmers expect a differentia! in

The price spreads report, which I have read carefully-and I have no doubt other hon. members have done the same- indicates clearly that the price spreads committee considered there was very little competition among the packers in the packing industry.
Here, again, we have the example at this time of one powerful packer speaking on behalf of the entire packing industry across the country. That looks as though what we have said so often in the house is perfectly true, and that is that the packing industry is a virtual monopoly controlled by one, or at the outside, two, of the great packing companies in this country.
I do net want to see a break in the price ceiling, because I know who would be the first to suffer. The first to suffer would be the pensioner, and other persons on fixed
incomes. And hardly less hit-perhaps indeed harder hit eventually-will be the primary producers and the wage and salary earners. Those are the classes which in the final analysis will suffer the most from the breaking of the price ceilings.
As I said a few moments ago, the point of attack as far as the government are concerned-is the manner in which they have permitted increases in the cost of farm production without making some adjustments to compensate the farmers. Lately I have been looking at the profits of the Massey-Harris company. The Financial Post indicates that the net profit of the Massey-Harris company for 1944 was $1,800,000. That is a considerable profit; indeed it is 80 per cent higher than the profit of the pre-war years which I admit immediately were low.

They will remember that that committee reported that prices of farm implements had been too high for the past thirty or forty years. The report stated that in the following years the farmers, in order to meet their machinery needs, would require to spend over $50,000,000 a year on agricultural implements.
That report was tabled in the house in 1937. Then v-ar broke out and very few farmers were able to buy implements. There was a period of six years when implements- I was going to say were non-existent- were in exceedingly short supply. Consequently the present backlog of farm implement needs is greater than it ever was in the history of this country. There is good business ahead for the farm implement companies. They have new and improved machinery, some of which was used for the manufacture of munitions but which can now be used to make farm implements. In some cases this machinery was installed by the government and has been no doubt obtained by the companies from the government at a great discount. They have more skilled technical workers; they have a greater demand; they have better machinery, and yet this is the time when we see a 12J per cent increase in the price of farm implements.
This rise in the value of the stocks from January to May may not have been due to any prior knowledge of a possible increase in the price of implements. I am not saying it was. but I am saying that they could have estimated that they would make more money and therefore that their stocks would be worth more. According to the information I have, they handed out 115,250 shares of stock at virtually S5 a share below what it was worth three months later. The Cockshutt company did much the same thing. They allowed two of their executives to buy 2,000 shares each during the next three years. In this case the option price was $9 a share and this stock also has sold up to approximately $20 a share.
Let us see what this means. Let us suppose that these individuals in the employ of the Massey-Harris company took up their one-third option in January. They could have taken up 38,000 shares. With the present price rise they would have made $190,000 if they had marketed their shares at the present figure.

That is the kind of thing that this house ought to take cognizance of. If I had been moving the resolution I would have moved it in entirely different terms. I would have moved it so that we would have criticized the government for having failed to grant comparable increases when prices of farm machinery and of other commodities that the farmer had to use were permitted to rise.
May I say to the ministers and to the government that when it is found necessary to do something with regard to the removal of price ceilings on a particular commodity or on a group of commodities, there should be no hole-in-the-wall negotiations. All the people concerned in the price rise should be called in. For example, in the case of farm implements the government should be represented; the farmer should be represented; the industrial worker should be represented, and the manufacturer should be represented. Perhaps we could then understand better why certain things are done, or perhaps in the light of day which wmuld be shed upon the matter the proposal would not be accepted and things like this would not happen. If we are to have price stabilization, let us have it.
If I might just consider another point. The other day the minister referred to increases in. prices of farm commodities during the past few years and set those up against the increase in the cost of farm machinery. Let me point out again that in 1937 the parliamentary committee tabled in this house a considered report containing voluminous information. It was an excellent report in many respects. That report stated that at that time prices of farm implements w'ere too high and that they had always been too high. We urged that something be done to cause the manufacturers to decrease these prices; in fact we recommended, among other things, that if they did not do so the government of this country should encourage the formation of farmers' coopera-
[Mr. Col dwell. |

lives for the manufacture and distribution of farm implements. We recommended that in the report.
I believe there are two or three ways in which this problem could be eased to some extent for the producers of this country. A publicly owned farm implement industry would be one way. We have the factories, the machines, and the labour. I know the government will not accept that. Then let me suggest that a thing which might be done is for the government to encourage the devolp-ment of a real cooperative farm implement industry in this country to give these private corporations some competition. If the government believes in the competitive system that is one way of giving these great organizations some competition. I want to point out that we cannot expect the farmers to accept price stabilization of the commodity they sell if they find that the commodities they buy are not to be stabilized and kept stabilized. There is the bald fact.
This amendment to-night is largely justified. I do not think it tackles the thing from the right end. I do not think it is the price ceiling policies with respect to farm products which are discouraging production, but, on the contrary, it is the permission to puncture price ceilings on the goods that the farmers buy that is the difficulty; and that is the angle from which I would tackle the matter.
Let me say again: in 1937 we repoi'ted that farm implement prices were high, that they should come down. The minister's argument the other day that farm prices had risen by so much per cent did not take into account the fact that no one in this house could say that agricultural prices in any year from 1931 to 1941 were high enough, that they covered the cost, of production. They did not. As I have told the house before, I have bought eggs at three cents a dozen in western Canada. True, that was not in 1939; that was in the spring of 1934. But in 1939 you could buy them at fifteen and twentj' cents a dozen. Wheat was around sixty cents a bushel, and other farm prices were on a somewhat similar level. Let us not compare 1939 farm prices with prices now and say, because there has been an increase in farm prices, therefore the increase in the price of farm implements is justified.
I do not want to say more about this at the moment, other than that if we are to have price ceilings let us have them for everybody, not pick somebody out and provide him with a hole in the ceiling. May I add that I believe we must have price ceilings. But we should receive proper representation from the people who are concerned. Who are
the people concerned? Of course the government is concerned, representing, as it should do, this parliament and the people of this country through this parliament; the producer is concerned; the worker is concerned, and I would say that under our present economic system the industrialist, the manufacturer, the owner of the plant is concerned. We should see to it that when we are going to set a stabilized price all the factors involved are studied and all those who have a stake in the price level are consulted.

The government says, "Well, now, we did a pretty good job there because, mind you, the machine companies wanted a 25 per cent increase and we gave them only 12% per cent." Of course, the machine companies never expected 25 per cent; that was a bargaining figure and they cut it to half knowing they were getting an extremely fine proposition at that.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke a moment ago about shooting at a stabilized price. I do not think there are many members here who are not desirous of having a stabilized price, but the government themselves are the ones who have been shooting at this price until now it is riddled, so that they had better put up another target. It is only reasonable to suppose-the government cannot expect anything else-that the farmer must continually shoot at that target, stabilized price. He is forced to do so. The farmer knows from past experience that the government will take no action whatever until it is forced to do so. There is clear evidence of that because in 1943 the farm organizations headed by the Saskatchewan wheat pool and supported by the Alberta and Manitoba wheat pools came to Ottawa and demanded increased prices for agriculture, and they were not received too well at that time. We shall not argue over ten cents one way or the other; maybe it was ninety cents.

Personally I think this government has done what I might call a noble job with this very difficult problem, with all the pressures that one feels sitting behind the desk, as I and the other members of the government do. I am sometimes twitted about the big interests. I do not think anyone can say I have been a friend of the big interests. I have always sat on the other side of the table, negotiating wage agreements; but you know you never take any chance in attacking the big interests. That is pie in the sky for the politician. There are not many of them. I have a vivid recollection of when I was a young member of this house, when the then leader of the government, who is known to most of us, was ill. I said to a friend of mine, "Do you think he is going to get well?" He replied, "Gosh, Humphrey, I hope he does. I have been shooting both barrels at him for the last four years, and if he dies I will have to switch to the banks." So that you get this exhibition of trying to please the greatest number, when in my judgment we should be giving them leadership. I agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Let us be fair about it; in a comparative sense this country is a paradise.
Perhaps it is not as good as it should be, but you see the difference when you look around the world, or even when you go across the border. The other day I was in a mediumsized city there, and I was amazed. I never thought the food situation and the price situation could ever reach the stage they have reached in the United States.

I just point out these things because, charged as I am with a very difficult problem, as are the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and the Minister of Agriculture and others, I hope we shall be able to maintain a reasonable price structure. I do not need to tell my farmer friends that I do not know much about agriculture, but I have lived through a couple of depressions and two wars. It is just like throwing a ball into the air; what goes up must come down. We all have a clear recol-

lection, of the price of wheat at the end of the last war, when it went up to something over $3 a bushel. We all remember that the price of land in western Canada increased tremendously. We all know what happened in regard to the production of wheat in France and Italy. Speaking from memory, the year before war broke out I believe Italy produced more wheat than Canada did, and that was largely brought about by the tremendous increase in the price level. In France they imposed a high tariff; in Italy they cleared marshland and grew wheat. I was in Paris is 1933, I believe, when the duty on a single bushel of wheat was about $1.25. That is an indication that unless we keep our feet on the ground and meet this very difficult period in a rational way, history is bound to repeat itself as surely as the sun will rise tomorrow morning.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) mentioned the people with fixed incomes. The other day I had an estimation made of the number of people drawing pensions from the state, from railway companies and so on, not including those in receipt of family allowances, and the number was about four hundred thousand, with another two million receiving family allowances. We all know that with every point increase in the price index the purchasing power of the income of what I call this great mass of defenceless people is reduced; and I think it is our duty, as it will always be mine while I am a member of this government, to see to it that this great body of people get the protection they are so richly entitled to and deserve.
I just wanted to say these few simple things, Mr. Speaker, in order that the people of this country might not be fooled by the arguments so often advanced by both sides into believing that there is no relationship between the price structure and the cost pf production. We all know there is a relationship and it must be worked out in a rational way. As far as human agencies go, I think it is a fair thing to say that the machinery developed in this country is as good as that in any other country. Following what was said about agricultural conditions, let me say that the wage index is the highest in the history of this country. That did not fall as a gentle rain from heaven. It was brought about by the organization of labour, of course, but also by the policies set in motion by this government.
In conclusion, I hope the people of this country will show the good sense that they have exhibited in the last four or five years, and see to it that we protect the living standards of the great mass of Canadian people which are predicated upon the maintenance of a price and wage stabilization policy.

, Mr. J. A. ROSS (Souris): Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the amendment may I point out, first of all, that matters connected with agricultural production are divided between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. The former has been responsible for production, and the latter for marketing; and in recent years, especially since 1941, under the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and Donald Gordon certain controls have been responsible for the hampering of agricultural production. When I mention these controls, I have said nothing about discriminatory income tax deductions which began to operate in 1942, and are still in existence.
I am sure all hon. members believe in a policy of stabilization. However, we believe it should be on a basis of parity, and I am convinced that many hon. members who rise in their places and support the government every time there is a vote, do not believe we have anything approaching parity under our present price control system.
For instance, speaking in this house on March 20 the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand) said:
The cost of living and the cost of farm production is still 22-6 per cent higher than the farmer receives for his products in this country.
The hon. member is a government supporter, but on that date he put those figures on Hansard.
Then, reference has been made to the increase in the price of gasoline. In the prairie provinces, drawing a line just west of Winnipeg, and including the three provinces, the order permitting the increase of two cents a gallon in the price of gasoline prevailed. When I first heard of this increase I wrote the Minister of Finance as follows, on February 28:
Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir:
I wish on behalf of the primary producers of the greater part of the prairie provinces to protest against the proposed increase of two cents per gallon on gasoline to take effect about the middle of Mhreh. This would seem very discriminatory and arbitrary. I suggest that proper investigation be made and reasonable explanation given to the public before the increase is allowed.
The minister was out of the country at that time, and as a result I received an acknowledgement of my letter from his secretary. The reply left the impression in my mind that the order was discriminatory. Reference was made in the letter to the oil fields of Montana, which were close to the prairie provinces. The letter went on to point out

that the subsidies would be continued from the southern states of Oklahoma and Texas, and that if these were eliminated and other regulations went into effect the price would probably increase by six cents a gallon. That was the reply I received, and certainly it indicates discrimination, and additional cost of production for the farmers of the prairie provinces.
On the matter of income tax deductions, at every session of parliament that I have attended I have tried to get some degree of fairness between the treatment accorded the farmer and his wife, and the man and wife who work in the city or in industry. I believe it was on November 30 of last year, if I remember correctly, that I asked the Minister of Finance if he had found a way of overcoming this discrimination. He explained that in 1942 the government had found it necessary to allow an extra $600 to the wife in industry connected with the war effort, which resulted in an amount of $1,800 for the married couple in industry or in the city as compared with $1,200 for the married couple on the farm. He knew it was wrong, and said that he was giving thought to it, but did not know whether he would be able to bring about a change in 1946.
Let me now deal with the increase of 12J per cent in the price of farm implements. I was not in the house in the debate respecting farm implements which took place on April 15, but I believe that upon that occasion a large part of the financial statement of the Massey-Ilarris company was placed upon Hansard. I worked for that company, selling machinery and making collections, in 1929 and 1930, and I know something about the percentage of their costs which go to sales, publicity and collections. None of those items of cost exist to-day, nor did they exist during the war. The company does not have to go out to sell machinery or to make collections, although in other years a large percentage of their cost was set aside and earmarked for that purpose. However, as I say, that does not apply to-day, nor did it apply during the years of war.
Let me give one concrete example of a further aggravation in connection with the implement business, with which the government is becoming entangled. Last fall, during harvest time, a man in my community found he was short of farm equipment. He had always used a certain type of equipment manufactured in the United States. This man wanted a ten-foot power binder, but it was not procurable at that time at any price. He did discover an extra binder in the city of Winnipeg. This was a Canadian type binder, manufactured in Canada. He could have procured the United States power binder delivered at Melita for about $395, had it been available, but had to pay $450 for the Canadian type of power binder. It will be understood that I am giving just round figures. However, the result was that he paid $55 more for the Canadian type of binder which he did not want, had he had a choice between the two types. Then, if we add 12J per cent to the price of the Canadian binder, we find it would now cost that man approximately $506, making a difference of $111 between the United States and Canadian prices.

The minister pointed out that this condition was brought about partly by the exorbitant prices paid at auction sales to-day. That is true; and those machine companies are taking advantage of the situation. With the knowledge that equipment is not available, in short supply, they are getting this increase, knowing that people must have machinery at any price. Surely the increase was most unfair.
At several points in the report of the parliamentary committee which investigated farm implement prices in 1937, the chairman of - the committee pointed out that farm machinery manufactured in Canada was altogether too highly priced for the farmers of' this country. If that was true then, when they had to pay for publicity, sales, collections and the like, which do not have to be paid to-day, certainly the present price is unwarranted and is a further aggravation of the situation faced by the producer.
I should like now to refer to an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on April 16, the day following the discussion on farm implement prices in the house. It says: Higher Prices for Farm Implements
If the Canadian government had gone out deliberately to create a storm of controversy in western Canada it could hardly have chosen a different instrument than the raising of farm implement prices.
The editorial is of considerable length, and the points are well discussed by whoever writes the editorials for that paper. I say that most certainly the increase, when it is added to the costs of agricultural production, will appear wholly unjustified. I do not know what it will lead to in the future.

Certainly he will,
when production becomes plentiful. But I am pointing out that the minister will have difficulty with the machinery companies then. To-day there is no choice. The farmers must buy where they can.
During the war the agricultural producers of Canada received less for their products than did the producers in any other of the united nations. As was pointed out this evening, prices of agricultural products in the United States are fifty per cent higher than in Canada on the average, while costs of the implements of production are less in the United States than they are in Canada.
1 did not know whether I should burden the house at this time with this matter, but during the Easter recess I drove across to the United States and interviewed several implement dealers. I got quite a list of farm implement prices. When I compared those with prices charged by comparable dealers on our side of the line I found that they were slightly under our prices. This wTas before the 124 per cent increase took place.
Some mention has been made of the price of wheat. According to an estimate made by the dominion bureau of statistics and based on the last grain crop, the prairie farmer would have received some $400,000,000 more if he had been allowed to sell at ordinary world prices such as prevailed on the Chicago grain market. The Canadian wheat crop was 305,000,000 bushels and the farmers were losing $170,000,000 on that crop. They were losing $135,000,000 on oats and $110,000,000 on barley. That is the difference between prices that prevail in the United States and what the farmer in Canada has received in one year.
According to a report tabled just a few days ago by Donald Gordon, it has cost this country some $322,000,000 to maintain price controls from December 1941 to date. When we consider the contribution of $400,000,000 which the farmer has made in one year because of reduced prices of grain I think we have proof that the 'agricultural producer of this country has made altogether too great a contribution in the way of subsidizing the

consumers of foodstuffs in Canada. As I say. this whole system has cost the taxpayers of this country many millions of dollars less to maintain since its inception on December 1, 1944 than the farmers have los't in one year.
The agricultural producer its entitled to the same consideration which has been given to to the lumber producer or the general manufacturer. They have been able to export their products at prevailing world market prices. Certainly there should be some basis of parity created in this stabilization system of ours. If that had been done, then many of the difficulties which faced the great dominion-provincial conference that took place in the other place last week would not have existed.
For instance, the budgets of the three prairie provinces amount to $102,000,000 annually. The budget of Manitoba is $22,000,000; Saskatchewan, $52,000,000, and Alberta, $28,000,000. The difference in prices received for grain by the western producer in one year is four times the entire annual budgets of the three prairie provinces. I believe there is some food for thought in those figures. If there had been some basis of parity the premiers of these prairie provinces would not have been so concerned about their future taxation problems.
The Minister of Agriculture said that he did not know how far back you would have to go to discover when the price of wheat was higher in Canada than it was in the United States. It is acknowledged that western Canada produces the finest cereals 'of any place in the world. I do not know how far back you could go, but I hold in my hand a copy of the chairman's report of the Canadian wheat board which was presented in 1919 by the then chairman, Mr. James Stewart, to the Right Hon. Sir George E. Foster, G.C.M.G., who was then Minister of Trade and Commerce. On page 5 of the report it is stated that the instructions given to the board at that time were as follows:
The instructions given to the Canadian wheat board were very simply stated. The board was instructed to sell the Canadian wheat crop of 1919 at a price which would bring the greatest possible benefit to the dominion as a whole.
That is the same period after the last war as we are now in after the war that has just ended. I think that is a very fair set of instructions. On the next page is given the personnel of the board that was set up. Practically all the principal vocations in Canada were represented on that wheat board, including official organized labour. That representative was satisfied at that time with the operations of this board. On another page it is pointed out that the average price throughout

those war years was twenty-five cents a bushel higher in Canada than in the United States. This is a government report. The report refers to one transaction in which wheat was exported from this country at $4.02 a bushel.
The price of wheat was set at $2.15 a bushel with participation certificates which, according to the report, gave another forty-eight cents a bushel to the producer, or a total of $2.63 a bushel. That was a higher price than ever prevailed in the United States at that time.
There is a comparison made of the prices of staple foodstuffs in these two great countries. As was pointed out this evening by my leader, the existing price of wheat to-day, including the thirty cent bonus, was practically $1 a bushel less in Canada than obtained at the point across the boundary in the United States. That is altogether too great a difference.
Mention has been made of beef prices. I have here the Winnipeg Free Press of April 27, which contains the headline, "Miles of St. Boniface pens empty." In one day the marketings amounted to only twenty-five cattle, and these are the greatest yards in the British empire where normally from 1.S00 to 2,000 head of cattle are received each day at this time of year, and contain facilities for handling many thousands a day.
Within a few days of the announcement of the increase in implement prices it was stated that they would not buy beef without decreasing the price approximately one cent a pound. Those who were caught with a supply of cattle on the market at that time took a loss of from $10 to $15 a head, but they had to do it. According to another bureau of statistics report, cattle prices on the Chicago market were almost one cent a pound higher at that time than they were one year ago. These two facts are strangely inconsistent. I have pointed out that implement prices did not rise throughout the war in the United States, according to the information I received from the implement dealers. In addition, beef prices were up almost one cent a pound over the previous year. In this country our farmers were faced with a decrease of one cent a pound in beef prices. This situation has greatly aggravated the position of the producer in this country.
I have dealt mainly with this matter from the western point of view, but something can be said for the eastern farmer. These men really have greater production difficulties in some respects than we in western Canada have. I have an account here which states that because of the shortage of farm labour and other difficulties in farm production 63260-80
100,000 acres in Simcoe county are lying idle. I am sure that other hon. members who are more conversant with conditions in the east will deal more ably with this problem. From what I have witnessed I believe they have many complex problems that even we in western Canada do not have, and everybody knows we have altogether too many. I am convinced that as a result many people are letting up on their production. Remember that the average age of farm operators in the prairie provinces to-day is over fifty-five years. They, their wives and those of their families that happened to be at home have worked long hours and done a magnificent job in producing for the war effort. They rightly think that, with the war over, they are entitled to lie back a bit and have some rest, and they would like to turn over a portion of their farms to the younger people. Strange as it may seem, some 7 per cent of the young people from the prairie provinces who enlisted in the services from farms have signified their intention to return to the farms; the others, the great majority, wish to try some other vocation, and with the difficulties which are arising to-day one con-not altogether blame them.
I have never missed an opportunity at any session since coming here in 1940 to ask for a basis of parity for agricultural producers in this country, based on their costs of production and living costs in this nation. At the last session, on September 25, I moved a resolution asking that the government should establish floor prices for all basic agricultural products at not less than 90 per cent of parity, and every supporter of the government rose in his place and voted against that resolution.
As I have pointed out, since then the United States have not altered the price of farm implements; they have added thirty cents a bushel bonus on wheat in recent days, while in the same recent days the Canadian government have increased the cost of farm implements, raised the cost of gasoline in most parts two cents a gallon, and, one would think, they are deliberately going out to make the lot of the agricultural producer in this country more difficult. I do not see how any hon. member who gives proper thought to this matter can oppose this amendment.

I am pleased because eventually he is learning something. He is agreeing with the policy which we of this group through

the past number of years have been advocating. I hope that his experiences will also lead him to admit the fallacy of the fire-sale policy which he had here some years ago.
As the representative of a rural constituency in a province that is more dependent upon the net return of agriculture than is any other province in Canada, I shall, of course, speak on behalf of the people whom I have the honour to represent. But let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, and all hon. members that I shall also endeavour to keep in mind the entire picture of our national economy, the welfare of our country as a whole.
In my opinion the government have no one to blame but themselves for the position they find themselves in,, because they refuse to go to the root of the trouble. Like the Bourbons of old, they forget nothing and learn nothing. They refuse to forget the heyday of their power. Sadder still, they refuse to recognize the fact that the day of so-called free competitive enterprise has long been over. They remind me of an old lady sitting in the glow of the fireplace spinning dreams of tho long, long ago and yet refusing to let the younger generation put the house in order.
For a year or more we from this side of the house have been urging the government to prepare plans for the post-war years, but all they have been able to accomplish is to get themselves into one impossible position after another. In fact, they remind me of the chap who got hold of the tail of one of those white-and-black striped pussies:	they are
afraid to let go and equally afraid to hold on. But this much they can be sure of, that, let go or hold on, the odour will be the same. Sooner or later they must let go. But before they do so, why not put an end to that robber of our national chicken-house, monopoly capitalism? Then, may I suggest to them that they bury that worn-out cloak of Liberalism. I see the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) who is always interested in dictionary definitions, so that he knows what I mean. I shall quote to him and for the benefit of the house the definition of "cloak" that I have found in Webster's dictionary:
1.	A loose outer garment. 2. That which conceals; blinds; disguise; mask. To cover with or as with a cloak; hide; conceal.
I hope the hon. member will understand what I refer to when I suggest to him to cast off the cloak of Liberalism.

Why should a nation whose people showed such williness to cooperate during wartime,
rMr. Burton.]
and by that cooperation achieved such wonderful success, now find it impossible to carry on with the same spirit of unity and cooperation in times of peace? My answer to that is, first, I am convinced that those unseen hands which control the economic life of this country are determined to force both farmer and labour back to the position in which we were in 1939; and, second-which in my opinion is even more serious-that in this day and age we have a government in office that not only condones the first, but also fails to recognize the fact that if one group in our national family is allowed to take more than its fair share of the national income, others must be getting less than their fair share.
WTiat this nation needs is a plan of action whereby everyone will be given an opportunity to do his or her best in the winning of the peace and at the same time have the assurance that a fair share of the fruits of his or her labours will be received. To do this, the government must give leadership; they must do away with the old method of pressure-group action and replace it with intelligent planning where representatives of farmer, labour, industry, consumer, in fact every group of our national life can meet in round-table conference, where with the help of facts and figures from our departmental experts we shall be able to plan a proper price structure, so that as nearly as possible everyone will receive a fair share of the national income. But, Mr. Speaker, that will not be possible unless the government are willing to let go of the tail of that so-called free enterprise. Nor will it be possible if they do let go, if they still allow that animal to destroy the last goose that lays the golden eggs.
People are demanding intelligent cooperative action. The time for royal commissions of inquiry is past, and so is the time for inquiries by committees. I say that because I have in my possession some copies of the report made by the committee of the House of Commons which was appointed to inquire into farm implement prices. I have here the conclusions and recommendations by the committee as will be found on pages 1294, 1295 and 1296, dated April 5, 6 and 7 of 1937.
Owing to the fact that many of us are beginning to find it very difficult to get copies of this report, I am going to ask your permission, Mr. Speaker, and that of the house to place on the record, without the necessity of reading them, the thirty-six points made by the committee in their conclusions and recommendations. I appreciate that more perhaps than I can say, especially in view of the fact that many of the younger people are beginning to farm and need implements, and in years gone by they did not have an opportunity really to know what the committee recommended at that time. The conclusions and recommendations by the committee in question are:
Conclusions and Recommendations by the Committee
(1)	That the prosperity of the farm implement industry is directly dependent on the prosperity of agriculture.
(2)	That, during the recent depression, a backlog of requirements estimated at $200,-
000.000 has accumulated and will have to he satisfied by the implement companies during the next few years, together with normal annual requirements of agriculture, estimated at $51,700,000.
(3)	That, as a result, the price level of farm implements during the next few years is of the greatest importance to agriculture.
(4)	That the companies engaged in the industry, over the period of their operations as a whole, have made substantial profits on the capital invested in each company.
(5)	That, if in particular instances this was was not so,' it was due to reasons other than the price level at which farm implements have sold in Canada throughout the same period.
(G) That the economic condition of agriculture is not satisfactory although the present relatively high prices for farm produce will tend to improve it, provided these continue and coincide with reasonably good crops.
(7)	That farmers have a right to expect the price level of farm implements to be based on the most efficient and economical manufacturing and distribution cost.
(8)	That from 1931 to 1934 inclusive, when all the companies incurred financial losses, such were due primarily to the inability of the farmer to purchase farm implements coupled with his inability to pay for those he had already purchased, and not to the fact that prices of farm implements were lower than justified by manufacturing or distribution costs.
(9)	That the unfavourable factors affecting the financial returns of the farm implement companies in the period 1930 to 1935 have been largely eliminated and therefore the companies can look forward to a period of relative prosperity in the industry.
(10)	That, particularly, the abnormal bad debt losses resulting from the depression have been largely absorbed by the implement companies and that this item of cost should not reappear in the next few years.
(11)	That freight rate increases have contributed to the increase in the price of farm implements.
(12)	That the matter of freight rates is of vital importance to the provinces more distant from the manufacturing centres and this is
63260-80^
emphasized by the fact that the three prairie' provinces absorb at least two-thirds of all farm implements sold in Canada.
(13)	That the matter of freight rates on farm implements should receive immediate attention with a view to restoring lower rates thereon.
(14)	That the relative increase in the cost of labour has been one of the important elements in the increase of prices occurring between 1913 and 1936.

May I add that that, in the opinion of many of us, these 'roots are the tentacles of a giant octupus which must be crushed if we are to have freedom of trade and a fair price structure.

I now come to recommendation No. 29, which reads as follows:
That the increases announced by the companies in January, 1936, were not justified by an increase in manufacturing or distribution costs or by the financial results of the companies in so far as these were affected by the price level of farm implements.
If they were not justified in receiving an increase at that time it is not fair or just to take the increase that we have had in the prices of farm products in recent years and compare it with the increase in manufactured goods, especially farm machinery, when we know that these companies have been charging more than they should have been. Recommendation No. 30 reads as follows: That over the period 1891 to 1936 retail prices of farm implements have been maintained at too high a level as shown by the financial returns to the companies engaged in the industry, during that period.
Then No. 32:
That after due consideration of all the essential factors, the committee is of the opinion that any suggestion of a further increase is not justified at the present time.
I wish that that committee had an opportunity to make a report at this time to see if they would not use a little more severe and stronger language.	*
Recommendation No. 33 reads as follows: That the committee is of the opinion that the cost of distribution of farm implements is unnecessarily high and constitutes an important factor in the prices to the consumers.

After this committee had made its recommendations, every effort was made to bring into existence a cooperative implement association, to get them going in the business, but no sooner were they in a position to commence'operations than we had regulations of one sort or another from the federal government which prevented their going ahead at that time. In 1944, farm implements increased from the dollar value of 1939 15-4 per cent higher; manufactured goods, 24-3 per cent; wages in agricultural industry, 52-5 per cent; and farm products, 60 per cent over the 1939 figure. In 1945, farm implements increased from the dollar value of 1939 only 8'9 per cent over the 1939 figure owing to the reduced tax. Those figures pretty well speak for themselves. The farmers had a pretty fair share of the income.
When it comes down to the talk about prices, and the fellows here are fighting for the strikers to get higher wages, it is all fine and dandy with me. But you people who represent farmers, which you pretend to do, will have to know that the same farmers will have to pay more for it.
Then, going back to the farm figures-and I do not like to disagree with the hon. member for Souris, because he has known me for a long time-

speechtext: When you were a Tory.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: We were on the executive of the union of municipalities, together. However, we do disagree to-night. The Liberals are in power; fine and dandy.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Not so good.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: The Conservatives were in power in 1933, and I will give something of what happened in those days.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Tell them, not us.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am going to compare values in 1929 with those of 1933 on farm products. We heard the hon. member for Souris say to-night that some days ago there were only twenty-five cattle on the market. But the price of cattle to-day is around $12 a hundred for top steers. Let us look back to 1933, when the Conservatives were in power, to see how much they could expect for their cattle in those days. Butcher steers were selling in 1929 at $10.16 per hundredweight, and the price in 1933 was $4.47. Hogs were selling in 1929 for $12.27 per hundredweight, and the average price in 1933 was

Price Ceilings-Farm Products

$5.54. I had five or six of them hanging up in my granary and I could not even sell them.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that owing to Mr. Bennett's high tariff butter went down in 1931 to a rock-bottom price of sixteen cents a pound.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Temiscouata knows, in many cases they were using butter for axle grease. We wish we had some on our table to-day. The 1929 price of butter was 39-3 cents a pound, and the average price in 1933 was 21 cents a pound. Eggs in 1929 sold for 48 cents a dozen, w'ith the 1933 price being 28 cents a dozen.
We are now getting into the matter which has taken up a considerable time in this house. Wheat No. 1 northern, basis Fort William, sold at $1.24 a bushel in 1929, while in 1933 it sold at the magnificent price of 54-3 cents a bushel. In 1929 oats sold for 58-8 cents a bushel; in 1933, 26-4 cents a bushel. Barley sold in 1929 for 7T5 cents a bushel and in 1933, 32-2 cents a bushel. The price of flax in 1929 was $2.02 a bushel; in 1933, 90 cents a bushel.
The reason for criticism from the other side is the reason I gave, a bid for power. The only reason I came here was to try to do something for Canada as a whole. I am not interested in power. I contend that the people of Canada were never better off financially in their lives. They would be satisfied to [DOT] have these prices stabilized over a period of years. I was instrumental in bringing about a stabilized price for wheat, and if we can stabilize prices of everything else we shall be happy for many years to come.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not in his seat at the moment because the last words I heard from my husband as I boarded the train at Broadview were not for me but for the minister.
I cannot tell him the message I got for him. There were other messages that I got for the minister which I also cannot tell him.
Everyone realizes at this time that there have been increases in the cost of the materials' and labour that go into the making of farm implements. A person would have to be very young indeed if he did not recognize this fact, but it is interesting to note that in the breakdown of the cost of a binder, according to the report issued in 1936, out of the price paid by the farmer at Regina of $281 there was only $22.62, or eight per cent, paid out in [Mr. Sinnctt.;
wages. Out of that $281 paid by the farmer, the cost of -materials was only $71.06, or 25 per cent. The combined cost of labour and material came to 33 per cent of the total cost to the farmer.
The other two-thirds of the cost were made up of other items such as overhead, experimental work, freight, commission and profit. What we should be asking now is whether there have been savings made in these other items that would help to compensate or offset the rise in the cost of materials and labour. I submit that there have been considerable savings to the companies on these various items.
Since the table was compiled in 1936, the price of binders has increased steadily. The same report tells us that the price jumped from $281 in 1936 to $324.75 in 1939, or an increase of 15 per cent. In addition to this increase, a new device was adopted for cutting losses on credit sales. This cut out the advantage to the buyer who paid cash and increased the cash price in order to make up for losses through time-payment sales. In other words, the cash customer carried the loss instead of the company.
If this was unfair in 1939, it is doubly unfair now in view of the fact that the pressure of demand at the present time results in cash sales in practically every case. The man who comes to have his name put on the waiting list for a binder, a tractor, a combine or a one-way now comes with cash in his hand, but he is still paying for the risk of the credit purchaser who has disappeared from the field. There has been no announcement that this charge has been removed from the books of the company when adding up costs
In the matter of credit collections, selling and collection expenses are given some attention in the report. The committee found:
There was a very decided duplication in selling and collection expense, all of which is reflected in the retail price. Each company has its own dealer organization, its own salesmen, its own collection agents, and its own service men which must be taken care of in the price paid by the farmers. The companies are inclined to agree with the above but insist that the industry does not see any way to effect a saving in these items of cost of distribution.
